input.question: What position does Friedrich von Amerling currently or formerly hold?

documents.text: In the opulent halls of the Habsburg Empire, where grandeur and artistry converged, Friedrich von Amerling, a master painter of his time, held a coveted position that few could rival. As the court painter to the Austrian imperial family, Amerling's brushstrokes danced across canvases, capturing the essence of royalty and nobility with unparalleled precision. Born in 1803, in Vienna, Austria, Amerling's artistic prowess was evident from a young age. His early training under the tutelage of Friedrich von Oelenhainz and Josef Klieber laid the foundation for his future success. However, it was his appointment as court painter that catapulted him to the pinnacle of artistic recognition. One of the earliest indications of Amerling's association with the imperial family dates back to 1824, when he received a commission from Emperor Francis I to paint a portrait of his daughter, Archduchess Marie Louise. This prestigious assignment not only showcased Amerling's exceptional skill but also marked the beginning of a long-standing relationship with the Habsburgs. As court painter, Amerling was tasked with capturing the likenesses of the imperial family, as well as notable dignitaries and aristocrats. His portraits, characterized by their subtlety and nuance, offered a glimpse into the private lives of the elite. Take, for instance, his 1832 portrait of Emperor Ferdinand I, which exudes a sense of quiet confidence and authority. The delicate play of light on the emperor's face, the intricate details of his attire, and the subtle expression of his eyes all attest to Amerling's mastery of his craft. Amerling's position as court painter also granted him access to the inner circles of the imperial court. He was a frequent guest at the Schönbrunn Palace, where he would attend lavish balls and receptions, rubbing shoulders with the crème de la crème of Viennese society. It was during one such occasion that he met his future wife, Antonie Kaltenthaler, a lady-in-waiting to the Empress. The artist's connection to the imperial family was further solidified through his involvement in various state occasions. In 1835, Amerling was commissioned to create a series of paintings commemorating the coronation of Emperor Ferdinand I as King of Hungary. These works, now housed in the Hungarian National Gallery, demonstrate Amerling's ability to capture the pomp and circumstance of royal events.
